title: Observational Evidence from Supernovae for an Accelerating Universe and a Cosmological Constant
authors: Riess et al. (High-z Supernova Search Team)
tldr: Distant exploding stars look fainter than they should, which means the expansion of the Universe is speeding up, not slowing down.

question.short: Is the expansion of the Universe slowing down, as gravity predicts?
question.detail: With matter alone, gravity should decelerate cosmic expansion. Measuring how much it has slowed tells us the Universe's contents and fate.

answer.short: No: expansion is accelerating, implying a cosmological constant (Ω_Λ > 0 at >99.7% confidence).
answer.detail: Distant supernovae are 10-15% farther than a low-density, matter-only universe allows. The authors are confident but flag dust and evolution as the main systematics to rule out.

why_important.headline: Decides the fate of the Universe
why_important.detail: Deceleration vs acceleration determines whether expansion ever stops.

why_important.headline: Tests whether Einstein's Λ is real
why_important.detail: A non-zero cosmological constant would mean empty space carries energy.

why_important.headline: Age-of-Universe tension
why_important.detail: Matter-only models gave an age younger than the oldest stars; acceleration could fix this.

background.headline: Type Ia supernovae as standard candles
background.detail: These explosions have nearly uniform peak brightness, so apparent brightness gives distance.

background.headline: Brighter ones fade more slowly
background.detail: The light-curve shape vs luminosity relation lets each supernova be calibrated to ~7% in distance.

background.headline: Earlier high-z hints
background.detail: A first small sample of distant supernovae had suggested a high-matter, decelerating universe.

background.headline: Nearby calibration sample
background.detail: Well-measured low-redshift supernovae anchor the distance scale.

method.headline: 16 distant + 34 nearby supernovae
method.detail: High-redshift (0.16 < z < 0.97) SNe Ia found with CTIO, followed up with HST and Keck.

method.headline: Two light-curve fitting methods
method.detail: MLCS and a template-fitting method independently convert light curves into distances.

method.headline: Compare distance vs redshift
method.detail: Fit the Hubble diagram to cosmological models with different Ω_M and Ω_Λ.

method.headline: Check dust, evolution, selection
method.detail: Colour-based extinction corrections and tests for systematic differences between near and far samples.

results.headline: Distant SNe 10-15% too far
results.detail: They are fainter than expected for a low-density universe with Λ = 0.

results.headline: Ω_Λ > 0 at 3.0-4.0σ
results.detail: Depending on method and sample, a positive cosmological constant is strongly preferred.

results.headline: Age ≈ 14.2 ± 1.7 Gyr
results.detail: Consistent with ages of the oldest stars, easing the earlier tension.

conclusion.headline: Universe is accelerating
conclusion.detail: Something with negative pressure, like a cosmological constant, dominates today.

conclusion.headline: Caveat: dust or SN evolution
conclusion.detail: Grey dust or brighter-in-the-past supernovae could mimic the signal; no evidence for either yet.

conclusion.headline: Small sample, more needed
conclusion.detail: Only 16 high-z objects; independent confirmation (e.g. CMB) is needed.

glossary.meaning: An object of known true brightness, so how bright it looks tells you how far away it is.
How much light is stretched by cosmic expansion; a proxy for distance and look-back time.
